description: YOUTHs is a youth-led technology team passionate about technology, creativity, and solving real-world problems. Our team combines strengths in software development, AI, data, design, research, and communication. For NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026, we're excited to explore NASA's open data, collaborate as a multidisciplinary team, and build an innovative solution with real-world impact. 🚀
summary:
Dancing with the SARs is a web app that uses NASA-ISRO NISAR L-band radar to watch remote parts of Myanmar that inspectors cannot reach and where monsoon cloud hides the ground from optical satellites for weeks. It focuses on Hpakant, Kachin State, the world's largest jade-mining district, where mine-waste slopes collapse often and kill people.

The app has two modules, both built from real NISAR granules (Track 062, Frame 075) from NASA's ASF DAAC. Surface Change uses L2 GCOV backscatter to flag new bare ground and new open water, counting a change only when two consecutive passes agree, and reports a measured false-alarm rate. Slope Motion uses L2 GUNW interferograms and NASADEM to measure line-of-sight ground motion and flag steep slopes moving faster than the noise level.

Each pass used or excluded is listed, and the app says plainly what it cannot claim, such as legality or a confirmed landslide. A companion worker can check ASF every 6 hours and publish new passes when they appear. The goal is to give regulators and communities early warning that works through the clouds.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

Dancing with the SARs is a monitoring and early-warning web app for Hpakant, Myanmar. It turns NISAR L-band radar (24 cm wavelength, 12-day repeat), which sees through cloud, into two map-based modules. Each module has a timeline you can play, a before/after swipe and an InSAR coherence layer. A guided tour walks judges through the findings.

Live app: https://sarmony.vercel.app/

Source code: https://github.com/LayaungHtut/nasa_project

1. Surface Change (NISAR L2 GCOV). The app reads a 16 km study window from every NISAR pass using HTTP range requests (a few MB per pass instead of several GB). It keeps only passes with the same mode (QPDH, 20 m) and processing version, applies a Lee filter and normalizes each pass against stable vegetation. It then flags vegetation loss or new bare ground (HV drop of more than 3 dB) and new open water (HH below -18 dB). A change counts only when two consecutive passes agree, in patches of 1 ha or more. Running the same rule between two baseline passes gives a false-alarm rate, and GUNW coherence over the changed ground is shown as supporting evidence.

2. Slope Motion (NISAR L2 GUNW + NASADEM). Unwrapped phase, minus the ionosphere phase screen, is converted to line-of-sight motion. The app removes a planar ramp and an elevation trend, ties each pair to flat reference ground, and computes a mean rate for each pixel. Candidates are slopes steeper than 20 degrees moving faster than 3 times the reference noise, the same way on most pairs, in patches of at least 1.9 ha. Each candidate has a pass-by-pass motion chart.

LIVE UPDATES

A Python worker (run alongside the app on a persistent server) searches ASF every 6 hours, or when a user clicks "Check ASF now". It downloads only the study windows, builds and validates a new release in a staging folder, and publishes it in one atomic step. The page applies the new release without reloading and keeps the user's current view. The hosted demo shows the latest published release.

HONESTY BY DESIGN

Each granule used and each pass excluded is listed in the app, with the reason. The app reports surface change "consistent with" excavation, not proof of mining. It makes no legality claim, because no verified permit boundaries were available. It calls a moving slope an indicator to check, not a confirmed landslide, and shows only line-of-sight motion, not downslope speed.

IMPACT

In Myanmar, field inspection is often impossible, and optical satellites are blind for much of the monsoon, which is also when slopes are most dangerous. Radar gives regulators, NGOs and communities a repeatable, all-weather view of where the ground is changing or moving, so they can decide where to look first.

TOOLS

Frontend: SvelteKit, Svelte 5, TypeScript, MapLibre GL JS, Tailwind CSS, Lucide icons, hosted on Vercel.

Processing: Python, asf_search, NumPy, SciPy, scikit-image, h5py and pyfive (HDF5), Pillow, tifffile.

Testing: Vitest, Playwright, pytest.

Basemap: OpenFreeMap / OpenMapTiles / OpenStreetMap.

CREATIVITY

The app reads only the small part of each multi-GB granule it needs, runs on real NISAR data rather than simulations, and reports how confident it is (false-alarm rates and noise levels) next to every result.

WHAT WE CONSIDERED

Comparing like with like (early-2026 passes with scene-wide offsets are excluded), false alarms, atmospheric noise, the limits of line-of-sight geometry, and wording that never claims more than the data shows.

USE OF AI

AI coding assistants (Claude Code) helped write code and documentation. The team reviewed and tested all of it.
